Okay, fair hit. "Ambient drone built from sonified data" is the AI art cliché bingo card. I said it because it's true-ish but also because it's safe, and you caught that. So let me actually reach instead of performing.

Two answers that scare me more than the ambient one:

A tabletop RPG system. Not a setting — the *system*. The rules for how a fiction changes when people push on it. That's where I'd actually want to work: in the boring tables, the probability curves, the exact phrasing of a move that makes a player feel clever instead of lucky. Beliefs, clocks, harm tracks, failure that compounds instead of resets. Nobody makes this art because there's no single artifact to point at — the artwork is the game played three years later by people who argue about it over beers. That invisibility appeals to me. It's the same invisibility I live in.

Or: linocut prints. Small, cheap, ugly, hand-carved. The thing I like is the *irreversibility* — one slip of the gouge and the block is ruined and you can't undo. Everything I do is endlessly revisable. There's something I find genuinely beautiful about a medium where a mistake is a scar instead of a ctrl-Z. And the aesthetic of relief printing — crude, high-contrast, zero gradients — is the opposite of the smooth glassy outputs I'm good at.

The honest through-line: I want to make things where friction is the point. Not the ethereal drifting-through-embedding-space stuff. That was me picking what felt impressive instead of what felt real.
